blocks.text: Alb. Schultens sought to confirm the same interpretation in his Animadverss. Philologg. in Iobum (which first appeared in 1709 and were reprinted in his Opera minora, Leiden 1769, p. 91. 92.) on ch. XL, 25, and on Proverb. XXX, 27, p. 258 f. of the Operr. minorr., and also in the Commentar. ad Proverb. p. 485, where he expresses the sense of this passage thus: the locust has no king, and yet this whole body divides the booty among themselves in equal portions, however dense and numerous it may be (for which reason it is called ארבה), so that this military and plundering throng seems to be held together as if under the strictest military discipline. But against this interpretation Schnurrer rightly objects, in my judgement, in his Animadverss. ad quaedam loca Proverbiorum Salomonis, contained in his collected Dissertations, p. 108 f., not only that it is rather inapt to say that the locusts go out allotting booty, since booty is not divided immediately upon going out, but also that it is evident that something is praised in the locusts as worthy of admiration which otherwise, in any multitude, could be brought about and maintained only through the supreme authority of a commander to whom all are subject. Now the division of booty is not of the class of things that can in no way be accomplished without a commander. If indeed the distribution of booty among many is to be equal and just, then it is certainly necessary that someone be present who can govern the whole affair by his authority and keep each and every one to his duty. But of this equality of distribution there is nothing in the context of the passage. Schnurrer himself, after refuting the interpretation of Hunt, who, drawing on the Arabic حضّ [ḥaḍḍa], to incite, renders our words: they go out into battle line, at the war-signal of their whole army, proposes this sense: The locusts indeed have no king, yet they all go out in haste, taking here that meaning of the Arabic verb חצץ which consists in hastening. For this could be mentioned of the locusts as something singular and worthy of admiration: that the column of an immense multitude, although subject to no one by whose command and authority it is ruled, nevertheless of its own accord so unites and holds together that, when it must advance into battle, absolutely all, with none resisting or delaying, show themselves most prompt and most ready. This interpretation of Schnurrer, however, though approved by Döderlein and Dathe, displeased Ziegler in his Notis ad vers. teuton. Proverb. p. 365, because haste would bring in the notion of disturbance and confusion, which ought to be entirely foreign to this image. Yet what Ziegler himself puts forward, that the words חצץ כלו are to be rendered either in heaps and in crowds or each in its own place, does not commend itself to me more; for I can hardly see how this sense can be drawn from the meanings of the verb حصّ [ḥaṣṣa] that he himself cites, 1) he divided, 2) he obtained by lot. I interpret the words חצץ כלו: its whole body dividing itself, namely into bands, which Jerome also expressed: it goes out [III, 280] entire by its bands; on which words Grotius aptly remarks: „It is an animal ἀγελαῖον [agelaion] (gregarious), but ἀβασίλευτον [abasileuton] (without a king), as we had of the ant above, VI, 7. Locusts go in a great cohort, says Pliny.“
Ludovicus de Dieu in Critica sacra on this passage.

For locusts drop down after sunset, since the cold deprives them of the power of flight, as Le Brun, an eyewitness (αὐτόπτης [autoptēs]), observes in Voyages au Levante, p. 252. To this Nahum III, 17 alludes: Your nobles are like locusts, and your princes like a great swarm of locusts, which, when it is cold, cling to the hedges; when the sun rises they fly away, so that it is not seen where they were. In this passage the opposite expression שמש זרחה, the sun rises, shows that יום קרה, the time of cold, is not the cold days at the beginning of spring, as Harmar contends in his Observatt. super Oriente vol. I, p. 203 ff., but the evening time, after sunset. On these words Jerome says: For this is the nature of locusts, that, torpid in the cold, they fly about in the heat.
